sectionB.q: 2. Name and define the basic divisions of Biology.
a: Zoology: study of animals.
Botany: study of plants.
Microbiology: study of microscopic organisms such as bacteria.

sectionB.q: 3. What is meant by Homologous and Analogous? Explain with examples.
a: Homologous structures have similar basic structure but different functions; e.g. the forelimbs of humans and other vertebrates.
Analogous structures have different structure but similar function; e.g. wings of a butterfly and wings of a bat.

sectionB.q: 4. Write Biological names of the following: (i) Onion plant (ii) Mango plant (iii) Neem Plant (iv) Frog (v) Cat (vi) House fly
a: Onion — Allium cepa.
Mango — Mangifera indica L.
Neem — Azadirachta indica.
Frog — Rana tigrina.
Cat — Felis catus.
Housefly — Musca domestica.

sectionB.q: 5. Explain the term Hypothesis with the help of an example.
a: A hypothesis is an intelligent, testable guess made by a scientist as an explanation of an observation.
Example from the textbook: after observing Plasmodium in malaria patients, the hypothesis was that Plasmodium is the cause of malaria.

sectionB.q: 6. Define Conservation of Biodiversity.
a: Conservation of biodiversity means protecting and preserving the variety of living organisms and their habitats so that threatened species and natural resources are maintained.
The textbook emphasizes habitat protection, reducing over-exploitation and controlling human activities that cause biodiversity loss.

sectionB.q: 7. Draw a neat and labelled diagram of Animal or plant cell. OR Draw a neat and labelled diagram of Cardiac muscles.
a: Diagram answer: draw the requested textbook diagram neatly and label the major structures.
For an animal cell, include cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi body, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, lysosomes and centrioles.
For cardiac muscle, show striations, nucleus, branching fibres and intercalated discs.

sectionB.q: 8. Define the following terms: (i) Diffusion (ii) Osmosis (iii) Facilitated diffusion
a: Diffusion: passive movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration.
Osmosis: movement of water from higher water potential to lower water potential through a selectively permeable membrane.
Facilitated diffusion: passive movement of specific substances across a membrane with the help of carrier proteins, without ATP.

sectionB.q: 9. Define two basic ways of cell death in multicellular organisms.
a: Apoptosis: programmed cell death involving a controlled sequence of physiological changes.
Necrosis: accidental cell death caused by external factors such as infection, toxins or injury.

sectionB.q: 10. Define Pulmonary circuit and Systematic circuit.
a: Pulmonary circuit: blood travels from the right ventricle to the lungs through pulmonary arteries and returns to the left atrium through pulmonary veins.
Systemic circuit: oxygenated blood travels from the left ventricle through the aorta to body organs and returns to the right side of the heart through the venae cavae.

sectionB.q: 11. What is the role of root in transportation of water and minerals.
a: Root hairs increase surface area for absorption.
Water enters mainly by osmosis and minerals may enter by diffusion or active transport.
Absorbed water and minerals pass through root tissues into the xylem and are carried upward as ascent of sap.

sectionB.q: 12. What disease are caused due to the deficiency of the following Vitamins: (i) Vitamin K (ii) Vitamin D (iii) Vitamin A
a: Vitamin K — bleeding disorder.
Vitamin D — rickets and osteomalacia.
Vitamin A — night blindness, eye infection and rough skin.

sectionB.q: 13. Write a note on Light microscope. OR Write three differences between Theory and Law.
a: Light microscope: uses visible light passing through the specimen; its magnification is obtained by combining the powers of the eyepiece and objective lens. Common total magnifications described in the textbook include 40×, 100× and 400×.
Theory: a well-tested, highly reliable scientific explanation of natural phenomena.
Law: a uniform or constant fact of nature; the textbook describes it as virtually irrefutable. A theory explains observations, while a law states a consistent fact or relationship.

sectionC.q: 14. What are plant tissues? Write their types and define any two.
a: Plant tissues are groups of plant cells with characteristic functions.
Two major categories are meristematic tissues and permanent tissues.
Meristematic tissues contain cells capable of division; apical meristem increases length and lateral meristem increases girth.
Permanent tissues arise from meristematic tissue and are unable to divide. They are simple or complex.

sectionC.q: 15. Draw neat and labelled diagram of Mitochondria.
a: Diagram answer: draw a double-membrane mitochondrion and label outer membrane, inner membrane, intermembrane space, cristae, matrix, ribosomes/granules and ATP synthase particles.
State that mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration and ATP production.

sectionC.q: 16. Define Mitosis, write its different stages, explain any two of them. OR Define Meiosis, Explain prophase and draw labelled diagram of it.
a: Mitosis is cell division in which one parent cell produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.
Prophase: chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane disappears and spindle formation begins.
Metaphase: chromosomes arrange at the equator.
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Telophase: chromosomes reach poles, nuclear membranes reform and two daughter nuclei develop.
Meiosis: a division producing four daughter cells with half the chromosome number; Prophase I is the long first stage in which homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs.

sectionC.q: 17. Write down two function of each of the following: (i) Oral cavity (ii) Stomach (iii) Liver
a: Oral cavity: receives and tastes food; saliva begins digestion and helps form food for swallowing.
Stomach: stores and mixes food; gastric digestion begins and proteins are acted upon by gastric enzymes.
Liver: produces bile for fat digestion; processes and stores nutrients and performs important metabolic functions.

sectionC.q: 18. Write any six differences between Respiration and Photosynthesis in plants.
a: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy; respiration releases chemical energy as ATP.
Photosynthesis occurs in chlorophyll-containing organisms; respiration occurs in all organisms.
Photosynthesis requires light; respiration does not require light.
Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; aerobic respiration mainly occurs in mitochondria.
Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water; aerobic respiration uses food molecules and oxygen.
Photosynthesis forms glucose and oxygen; aerobic respiration forms carbon dioxide and water.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart and generally have thick, elastic muscular walls.
Veins carry blood toward the heart and have thinner walls; valves help prevent backflow.
Capillaries are very narrow vessels with thin walls where exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes occurs between blood and tissues.

sectionB.q: 2. Define the following: (i) Parasitology (ii) Environmental Biology (iii) Biotechnology
a: Parasitology: study of parasites.
Environmental biology: study of relationships between organisms and non-living environmental factors.
Biotechnology: techniques for manipulating genes to obtain desirable characteristics or useful products.

sectionB.q: 3. Explain the biological method with the help of a flowchart.
a: Biological problem → related observations and previous knowledge → hypothesis → inductive/deductive reasoning → experiment → data collection and analysis → theory when supported.
A hypothesis is tested by experiment; results are analyzed and a conclusion is reached.

sectionB.q: 4. Describe any three principles of classification.
a: Morphological characters: organisms are compared using form and structure, including homologous and analogous structures.
Cytological characters: classification considers cellular characteristics.
Genetic characters: organisms are compared on the basis of genetic constitution; the textbook also notes biochemical evidence.

sectionB.q: 5. Write any three differences between light microscope and electron microscope.
a: Light microscope uses visible light; electron microscope uses a beam of electrons.
Light microscope generally has lower resolution; electron microscope gives much higher resolution.
Light microscope can be used to observe living specimens under suitable conditions; electron microscopy generally requires specially prepared specimens.

sectionB.q: 6. Write different types of chromosomes with their diagrams.
a: Metacentric: centromere produces approximately equal arms.
Submetacentric: arms are unequal.
Acrocentric/sub-telocentric: one arm is very short and the other very long; centromere is subterminal.
Telocentric: centromere is at the end.
Draw four labelled chromosome shapes beside the definitions.

sectionB.q: 7. Define mitosis
a: Mitosis is a type of cell division in which a parent cell divides to form two daughter cells having the same chromosome number as the parent cell.

sectionB.q: 8. Write any three effects of malnutrition on human.
a: Starvation: severe deficiency of caloric energy.
Heart disease: an unbalanced diet and excess fatty food may increase cardiovascular risk.
Constipation: difficulty in emptying the bowel.
Other textbook effects include obesity and increased risk of infection.

sectionB.q: 9. Draw a neat and labelled diagram of 'Amoeba'.
a: Diagram answer: label cell membrane, ectoplasm, endoplasm, nucleus, food vacuole, mitochondria and pseudopodia.
Amoeba is unicellular and moves using pseudopodia.

sectionB.q: 10. Describe any three causes of deforestation.
a: Mining.
Paper making and timber extraction.
Urbanization and road construction.
Agricultural expansion and livestock breeding are also listed in the textbook.

sectionB.q: 11. Write down any one function each of the following: (i) Mitochondria (ii) Golgi Bodies (iii) Plastids
a: Mitochondria: site of aerobic respiration and ATP production.
Golgi bodies: modify, sort and package proteins into vesicles.
Plastids: manufacture/store important chemical compounds; chloroplasts also carry out photosynthesis.

sectionB.q: 12. Write down any three characteristics of kingdom Fungi.
a: Fungi are eukaryotic and generally multicellular.
They are achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs.
Their cell wall is mainly made of chitin.
Their body is a mycelium made of thread-like hyphae.

sectionB.q: 13. 'Careers in Biology'. Describe any three fields of it.
a: Medicine and surgery: diagnosis/treatment of diseases and repair or removal of affected organs.
Agriculture: production of crops, fruits, vegetables and dairy products.
Horticulture: development of new plant varieties and products.
Other textbook careers include forestry, farming, animal husbandry, fisheries and biotechnology.

sectionC.q: 14. Draw a neat and labelled diagram of Human Alimentary canal OR internal structure of Human Heart.
a: Alimentary canal diagram labels: oral cavity/mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus; also label liver, gall bladder and pancreas.
Heart diagram labels: right/left atria, right/left ventricles, septum, tricuspid and mitral valves, pulmonary artery/veins, aorta and venae cavae.

sectionC.q: 15. Write the name of two blood diseases. Describe their symptoms and causes.
a: Leukemia: blood cancer involving abnormal blood-cell production. Textbook symptoms include persistent weakness/fatigue, frequent infections, swollen lymph nodes and abnormal bleeding. Causes are associated with mutations and may include genetic and environmental factors listed in the text.

Thalassemia: inherited disorder affecting haemoglobin production. Symptoms include pale appearance, poor appetite, slowed growth, dark urine and enlarged spleen/liver/heart. It occurs because abnormal genes are inherited from parents.

sectionC.q: 16. Define the following terms: (i) Vitamins (ii) Goiter (iii) Stomata (iv) Nucleoplasm (v) Cisternae (vi) Activator
a: Vitamins: organic micronutrients required in small quantities for normal metabolism, health and development.
Goiter: enlargement/swelling of the thyroid gland, caused in the textbook by insufficient iodine.
Stomata: pores in plant surfaces surrounded by guard cells and involved in gas exchange/transpiration.
Nucleoplasm: granular fluid present inside the nuclear envelope.
Cisternae: flattened hollow folds/sacs of the endoplasmic reticulum; Golgi bodies also consist of stacked cisternae.
Activator: a substance that enhances enzyme activity.

sectionC.q: 17. What are the major components of human food? Describe any two components.
a: The textbook lists seven major nutrient classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, minerals, fibres, vitamins and water.
Carbohydrates: major energy source; include sugars, starches and fibres.
Proteins: made of amino acids and needed mainly for growth and repair of tissues.
Fats: made of fatty acids and glycerol; provide energy, growth support and insulation.

sectionC.q: 18. Define enzyme. Write any four characteristics of it.
a: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy.
They are not consumed during the reaction.
They are highly specific in action and act on particular substrates.
They have an active site where the substrate attaches.
Their activity is affected by temperature, pH and substrate concentration.
Some require cofactors; activators can enhance activity and inhibitors can decrease it.

sectionC.q: 19. Write any six differences between respiration and photosynthesis in plants.
a: Photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy; respiration releases energy as ATP.
Photosynthesis occurs in chlorophyll-containing organisms; respiration occurs in all organisms.
Photosynthesis needs light; respiration does not.
Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; aerobic respiration occurs mainly in mitochondria.
Photosynthesis uses CO2 and water; aerobic respiration uses food and oxygen.
Photosynthesis produces glucose and oxygen; aerobic respiration produces CO2 and water.

sectionB.q: 2. Write the contribution of any three Muslims scientist in the field of Biology.
a: Jabir Bin Hayan: wrote books on plants and animals, including Al-Nabatiat and Al-Haywan.
Abdul Malik Asmai: a zoologist who wrote works on horses, camels, sheep, wild animals and the human body.
Bu Ali Sina (Avicenna): regarded by the textbook as a founder of medicine; identified diseases such as tuberculosis and meningitis and wrote Al-Qanoon and other works.

sectionB.q: 3. Write three fundamental postulates of cell theory.
a: All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of living organisms.
New cells arise from pre-existing cells by cell division.
The textbook also states that cells contain hereditary material passed from generation to generation.

sectionB.q: 4. Draw neat and labeled diagram of smooth Muscles.
a: Diagram answer: show elongated spindle-shaped fibres, non-striated cytoplasm and a central nucleus.
Smooth muscle is involuntary and is found in walls of blood vessels and digestive tract and other internal structures.

sectionB.q: 5. Define Biodiversity and its importance.
a: Biodiversity is the degree of variation within or among species in different regions of Earth.
It provides products such as food, fibre, oil, rubber, timber and medicines.
It stabilizes ecosystems by recycling nutrients and helps reduce pollution; it also supports tourism and natural resources.

sectionB.q: 6. Differentiate between any one of the following: (i) Law and Theory (ii) Horticulture and Agriculture
a: Theory: a well-tested scientific explanation of natural phenomena. Law: a uniform or constant fact of nature.
Agriculture: production of crops, fruits, vegetables and dairy products. Horticulture: a part of agriculture concerned with development of new varieties of plants and their products.

sectionB.q: 7. Define plastids and write its types.
a: Plastids are major cytoplasmic organelles of plants and algae involved in manufacture and storage of important compounds.
Types: chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
Chloroplasts contain green pigment; chromoplasts contain coloured pigments; leucoplasts are colourless.

sectionB.q: 8. Define: (i) Arteries (ii) Veins (iii) Capillaries
a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
Veins carry blood toward the heart.
Capillaries are tiny thin-walled vessels where exchange between blood and tissues occurs.

sectionB.q: 9. Write the translation of any two Quranic Ayah about plants and animals.
a: Surah Al-Anbiya 21:30 — the textbook gives the meaning that every living thing was made from water.
Surah Al-Nur 24:45 — the textbook explains that Allah created animals from water and describes animals that move on their bellies, on two legs and on four legs.
Surah Al-Ra'd 13:4 describes neighboring land, vineyards and date-palms that are watered with the same water yet differ in fruit; the textbook relates it to plant growth and development.

sectionB.q: 10. What is photosynthesis? Explain it with chemical equation.
a: Photosynthesis is the process in which chlorophyll-containing organisms use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O —light/chlorophyll→ C6H12O6 + 6O2.
The textbook states that photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy and produces glucose as the fundamental organic product.

sectionB.q: 11. Why is Meiosis called reduction division?
a: Meiosis is called reduction division because the chromosome number is reduced to half during Meiosis I.
One diploid cell ultimately produces four haploid daughter cells.
Reduction maintains the chromosome number of a species after fertilization restores the diploid condition.

sectionB.q: 12. Define the following terms: (i) Vitamins (ii) Ulcer (iii) Anemia
a: Vitamins: organic micronutrients needed in small quantities for normal metabolism, health and development.
Ulcer: a lesion/erosion of the stomach or digestive lining; the textbook describes abdominal burning/pain and other digestive symptoms.
Anemia: a condition in which red blood cells or haemoglobin are below normal, reducing oxygen supply to body cells; iron deficiency is a major cause described in the textbook.

sectionB.q: 13. Write note on Mitochondria
a: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles with outer and inner membranes; the inner membrane forms cristae surrounding a matrix.
They are the site of aerobic respiration and ATP production, so they are called the powerhouse of the cell.
The cristae contain proteins involved in ATP synthesis.

sectionC.q: 14. Draw a neat and labeled diagram of Internal structure of Human Heart.
a: Label four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.
Also label septum, tricuspid valve, mitral/bicuspid valve, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta and superior/inferior vena cava.
Show the direction of blood flow from body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body.

sectionC.q: 15. Define Respiration. Write aerobic and anaerobic respiration with chemical equations.
a: Respiration is the breakdown of food molecules in cells to release energy.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and ultimately forms carbon dioxide and water: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP).
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen; in the textbook, fermentation may produce lactic acid or ethanol and CO2 depending on the organism.
Glycolysis produces pyruvic acid and a small ATP yield; aerobic respiration continues through Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.
Robert Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom system in 1969 based mainly on cellular organization/body organization and mode of nutrition.
Monera: prokaryotes such as bacteria and cyanobacteria.
Protista: mainly unicellular eukaryotes such as protozoa and unicellular algae.
Fungi: achlorophyllous absorptive heterotrophs with chitinous cell wall.
Plantae: multicellular eukaryotic photosynthetic organisms with mainly cellulose cell walls.
Animalia: multicellular eukaryotic ingestive heterotrophs without cell walls.

sectionC.q: 17. What is blood? Explain main components of blood with diagram.
a: Blood is a fluid connective tissue that transports substances through the body.
Its two main parts are plasma and corpuscles.
Plasma is the fluid part containing dissolved substances and proteins.
Corpuscles include red blood cells and white blood cells; platelets are cell fragments involved in clotting.
Diagram should label RBCs, WBCs, platelets and plasma.

sectionC.q: 18. What is tissue? Point out plant tissues with the help of flow chart.
a: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a common function.
Plant tissues → Meristematic tissues + Permanent tissues.
Permanent tissues → Simple permanent tissues + Complex/compound tissues.
Simple examples: epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma. Complex tissues: xylem and phloem.

sectionC.q: 19. Define mitosis. Name and define different stages of it with diagram of each.
a: Mitosis is cell division producing two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible; spindle forms and nuclear membrane disappears.
Metaphase: chromosomes arrange on the equator.
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
Telophase: chromosomes reach poles and nuclear membranes reform.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to form two daughter cells. Draw and label each stage.

sectionB.q: 2. Define: Paleontology, Environmental biology, Genetics.
a: Paleontology: study of remote past organic life with the help of fossils.
Environmental biology: study of relationships between living organisms and non-living environmental factors.
Genetics: study of heredity and transfer of characters from parents to offspring.

sectionB.q: 3. Draw a neat and labelled diagram of Animal cell.
a: Diagram answer: label cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi body, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes, lysosomes and centrioles.
Show the nucleus with nuclear envelope, nucleoplasm and nucleolus where appropriate.

sectionB.q: 4. Define classification. Names units of it and explain any one.
a: Classification is arranging organisms into groups on the basis of similar and dissimilar characteristics so they can be studied and identified easily.
Taxonomic units: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
Species is the smallest and basic unit; members share fundamental similarities and can naturally interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

sectionB.q: 5. Describe the relationship of Biology with any three branches of science.
a: Biophysics applies laws and techniques of physics to life processes.
Biomathematics/Biometry applies mathematics to collecting and analyzing biological data.
Biochemistry combines biology and chemistry to study molecules forming living organisms and cells.

sectionB.q: 6. Define plastids and write two types of it.
a: Plastids are major plant/algal organelles involved in manufacture and storage of important compounds.
Two types: chloroplasts and chromoplasts. The textbook also lists leucoplasts as a third type.

sectionB.q: 7. Write three differences between prokaryotic cell and eukaryotic cell.
a: Prokaryotic cells lack a true membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a proper nucleus.
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes possess them.
Prokaryotic organization is simpler; eukaryotic cells have more complex internal organization.

sectionB.q: 8. Define chromosome. Name the types of it.
a: Chromosomes are thread-like structures that appear during cell division and contain hereditary genes.
They are made of DNA and histone proteins.
Types based on centromere position: metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric/sub-telocentric and telocentric.

sectionB.q: 9. Define enzyme. Write any two uses of enzymes.
a: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy.
Industrial uses include food/bakery processing, brewing and bio-detergents; the textbook also mentions paper industry applications.

sectionB.q: 10. Write three differences between light reaction and dark reaction.
a: Light reaction requires light; dark/light-independent reaction does not directly require photons.
Light reaction occurs at thylakoid membranes; dark reaction occurs in the chloroplast stroma.
Light reaction produces ATP and NADPH2; the dark reaction uses these energy-rich compounds to synthesize glucose from CO2.

sectionB.q: 11. Define heterotrophic nutrition and explain its types.
a: Heterotrophic nutrition is obtaining nutrients from other sources because the organism does not synthesize its own food.
Heterotrophic modes described in the textbook include parasitic, saprotrophic and holozoic nutrition.
Herbivores obtain food from plants; carnivores consume animals and their products.

sectionB.q: 12. Define vitamin and explain its two types.
a: A vitamin is an organic micronutrient needed in small quantities for proper metabolism, health and development.
Fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in fats and include A, D, E and K.
Water-soluble vitamins dissolve in water and include B and C; the textbook notes that cooking/heating can destroy these more readily.

sectionB.q: 13. Write any three effects of malnutrition on human.
a: Starvation due to severe caloric deficiency.
Heart/cardiovascular disease associated with an unbalanced diet and excess fatty food.
Constipation due to difficulty in bowel emptying.
Other textbook effects include obesity and increased risk of infection.

sectionC.q: 14. Draw a neat anti labelled diagram of human alimentary canal.
a: Draw and label oral cavity/mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.
Also label accessory organs shown in the textbook: liver, gall bladder and pancreas.
Show the alimentary canal as the continuous tube from mouth to anus.
